# Load the dataset

```{r}

data(mtcars)

# Display the first six observations
head(mtcars)
```

# Data Exploration

```{r}
# Check data structure
str(mtcars)

# Select relevant variables
data <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")]

# Summary statistics
summary(data)

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(data))
```

# Data Visualization

```{r}
# Relationship between weight and fuel efficiency
plot(data$wt, data$mpg,
     main = "Weight vs Fuel Efficiency",
     xlab = "Weight",
     ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     pch = 19)

# Relationship between horsepower and fuel efficiency
plot(data$hp, data$mpg,
     main = "Horsepower vs Fuel Efficiency",
     xlab = "Horsepower",
     ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     pch = 19)
```

# Multiple Linear Regression Model

The regression model is:

MPG = β0 + β1(WT) + β2(HP) + ε

```{r}
# Fit the regression model
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = data)

# Display regression results
summary(model)
```

# Interpretation of Results

```{r}
# Extract regression coefficients
coef(model)

# Display R-squared
summary(model)$r.squared

# Display adjusted R-squared
summary(model)$adj.r.squared

# Display F-statistic and p-value
summary(model)$fstatistic
```

The regression equation is approximately:

MPG = 37.227 - 3.878(WT) - 0.032(HP)

Interpretation of Results

- Intercept (37.227): Expected fuel efficiency when weight and horsepower are zero.
- Weight (-3.878): Increasing weight by 1,000 pounds reduces fuel efficiency by 3.878 MPG.
- Horsepower (-0.032): Increasing horsepower by one unit reduces fuel efficiency by 0.032 MPG.
- R-squared (82.68%): Weight and horsepower explain 82.68% of the changes in fuel efficiency.

#Regression Diagnostics

Regression diagnostics help assess whether the assumptions of multiple linear regression are satisfied.

```{r}
# Display diagnostic plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

#Normality Test

```{r}
# Shapiro-Wilk normality test
shapiro.test(residuals(model))
```

Interpretation:

If the p-value is greater than 0.05, there is insufficient evidence to reject the assumption of normally distributed residuals.

# Multicollinearity Test

```{r}
# Correlation between independent variables
cor(data$wt, data$hp)
```

A high correlation may indicate multicollinearity between the independent variables.

# Homoscedasticity Test

```{r}

library(lmtest)

# Breusch-Pagan test
bptest(model)
```

Interpretation:

- p-value greater than 0.05: No significant evidence of heteroscedasticity.
- p-value less than 0.05: Evidence of heteroscedasticity.

# Prediction

```{r}
# Predict fuel efficiency for a vehicle
new_car <- data.frame(wt = 3.0, hp = 120)

predict(model, newdata = new_car)
```

This predicts fuel efficiency for a vehicle weighing 3,000 pounds and having 120 horsepower.

#Conclusion

The results show that heavier cars and cars with higher horsepower use more fuel. Our model explains 82.68% of the differences in fuel efficiency. This shows that multiple linear regression helps us understand how several factors affect one outcome.
